I am seventy-three years old, and I have walked these 4.1 mu for fifty-five years. My back is bent, but my hands remember the work. With seven people in the house and my sons off at factories, I farm mostly with my wife and daughter-in-law. My well has never run dry, and that water is the reason my crops survive when the sky forgets to rain.

This year, I will keep 2 mu in the wheat-maize rotation that has fed us for generations. The winter wheat is already in the ground from last autumn. I will top-dress it with urea when it greens up and irrigate four times—winter water, jointing water, heading water, and grain-filling water. I rotary till before planting each year. After the June harvest, I immediately plant hybrid maize on that same 2 mu. There is no time to waste between crops, so I will use no-tillage planting to save moisture and labor. Maize only needs two irrigations in summer if the rains come, and the hybrids give good ears.

Cotton is my cash crop, and I will give it 1.5 mu. I plough deep for cotton because its roots need loose soil to breathe. I buy improved Bt cotton seed from the county supply shop. Cotton is hungry—especially for potassium—so I give it more fertilizer than the grain crops. I irrigate four times, at seedling, budding, flowering, and boll-setting. I spray pesticides five times because even Bt cotton cannot stop every aphid and mite. Picking is hard on my old fingers, but the seed cotton brings in cash for medicine and the grandchildren’s school fees.

The remaining 0.6 mu is stevia. I planted it two years ago, and it comes back on its own. It is light work compared to cotton. I spread some fertilizer, irrigate three times, spray twice for insects, and cut the sweet leaves in summer. It does not fill our bellies, but the county buyer pays cash for it.

I use improved seed for wheat, cotton, and stevia because the county agricultural office showed me they fight disease better. For maize, hybrid seed is the only choice—open-pollinated maize disappeared from our village long ago. I till deep for cotton, rotary till for wheat and stevia, and leave the maize ground alone after wheat harvest.
